nodes.label: Campus Area Network (CAN)
nodes.description: A computer network made up of interconnected LANs within a limited geographical area; larger than a LAN and smaller than a MAN or WAN.

nodes.label: Wide Area Network (WAN)

source_claims.claim: A campus network/CAN is an interconnection of LANs within a limited geographical area.
CAN is larger than LAN and smaller than MAN or WAN.
Campus networking equipment and transmission media are almost entirely owned by the campus tenant/owner.
University CANs interconnect many categories of buildings and outlying structures.
SUNet, Project Athena, and Andrew are cited as early examples.
Corporate campus networks connect buildings, with Googleplex and Microsoft campus given as examples.
Campus networks are normally interconnected using high-speed Ethernet over optical fiber, including Gigabit and 10 Gigabit Ethernet.
The source states a CAN range of 1 to 5 km (1 to 3 miles).
The source states that connected buildings in the same domain can constitute a CAN.
The article cites networking textbooks and institutional/historical references.
CAN appears in a taxonomy of computer network types by scale and other dimensions.
The source specifically associates corporate CANs with high-speed links.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: CAN interconnects LANs across a limited campus area; LAN is one constituent local network.
The source places CAN below MAN in scale.
The source places CAN below WAN in scale.
The source presents these as alternative terms rather than distinct technologies.
Switches/routers are active networking equipment; fiber/copper/Cat5 are transmission media.
Both connect buildings, but the source gives different organizational contexts and examples.
Both are named CAN media; fiber is specifically associated with the high-speed Ethernet corporate pattern.
Both are examples of high-speed Ethernet; the source distinguishes them by named link speed.
The source provides both a numeric range and a domain/connectivity condition; these are different classification dimensions.
CAN is a campus network scope; backbone is a network type listed separately in the taxonomy.
The taxonomy mixes geographic scale categories with categories such as SAN, WLAN, VLAN, and LPWAN.
The source emphasizes campus ownership of infrastructure rather than an externally owned access network.

misconceptions.misconception: CAN is just a larger single LAN.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines CAN as an interconnection of LANs, so its defining structure is aggregation/interconnection of local networks.

misconceptions.misconception: CAN is larger than a MAN.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly states CAN is smaller than MAN.
The source emphasizes switches, routers, optical fiber, copper plant, and Cat5 cabling; wireless is not required by this definition.

misconceptions.misconception: CAN equipment must be externally owned.
misconceptions.correction: The source says equipment and transmission media are almost entirely owned by the campus tenant/owner.
The source explicitly includes enterprise, university, and government ownership/use contexts and discusses corporate campuses.

misconceptions.misconception: A CAN has to use fiber.
misconceptions.correction: Fiber is one named medium; copper plant and Cat5 are also explicitly named.

misconceptions.misconception: Every campus CAN must use 10 Gigabit Ethernet.
misconceptions.correction: 10 Gigabit Ethernet is one example of high-speed Ethernet, alongside Gigabit Ethernet.

misconceptions.misconception: The 1–5 km figure is an absolute universal standard.
misconceptions.correction: The source states this range but marks the associated statement with a citation-needed note; it should be treated as source-provided rather than a universal engineering rule.

misconceptions.misconception: Campus network and corporate area network are completely different technologies.
misconceptions.correction: The source presents campus network and corporate area network as alternative terminology for CAN.

misconceptions.misconception: A CAN is the same thing as the Internet.
misconceptions.correction: CAN is a limited-area network interconnecting LANs; the Internet is separately listed as a much broader network category.
